title: A few shortcuts shrink the world
hook: Add a handful of long links to a ring of 100 people. How much closer does everyone get?

knows: people can be linked, and a step is one link
doesNotKnow: a handful of random long links nearly halves the typical distance (and more with a few more)

misconception: To shrink distances you must rewire a large part of the network.
objective: The learner can explain that adding a few random long-distance links to a ring of local friendships cuts the average number of steps between two people by nearly half with 5 links (12.9 to 6.8, a 47% cut) and by almost two-thirds with 20 (4.9).

claims.text: With no shortcuts the average is 12.9 steps; with 5 and with 20 shortcuts in the lesson's seed-1 world it is 6.8 and 4.9 steps (12.88, 6.78 and 4.85 before rounding; 1 shortcut: 10.34).
claims.source: model.ts: ring of 100, each linked to the 2 people on each side (ring distance 1 and 2); shortcuts drawn by mulberry32(1): pick two people uniformly (randInt 0..99 twice), skip if equal or already linked, repeat; the first 1, 5, 20 pairs of that one sequence are nested. Average steps = exact all-pairs BFS over all 9,900 ordered pairs. Re-run in node 2026-10-14: 12.8788, 10.3436, 6.7810, 4.8539. Seed 1 is the first seed tried (not tuned). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Ran the lesson's model.ts (fc/sw.mjs): 12.8788, 10.3436, 6.7810, 4.8539; shortcuts nested (first 5 of the 20 identical). Predict "12.9" and answer "7 steps" match.

claims.text: Other seeds differ a little: over seeds 1 to 20 the average with 5 shortcuts is 7.38 steps (range 6.38 to 8.29) and with 20 shortcuts 4.69 (4.47 to 4.86).
claims.source: Same rule as c1, seeds 1..20, mean of the average steps, re-run in node 2026-10-14. Reveal says only 'other seeds differ a little'; the figures are the evidence. Answer B (about 7) holds for the seed-1 world (6.78) and for the 20-seed mean (7.38). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Seeds 1-20: 5 shortcuts mean 7.382 (6.380 to 8.291); 20 shortcuts mean 4.689 (4.474 to 4.857).

claims.text: Clustering (the share of a person's contacts who know each other, averaged over people) is 0.500 with no shortcuts and 0.435 with 20 shortcuts in the seed-1 world (0.496 with 1, 0.480 with 5).
claims.source: model.ts clustering(): for each person, links among their contacts divided by pairs of contacts, averaged over the 100 people. Re-run in node 2026-10-14 for seed 1: 0.5000, 0.4960, 0.4800, 0.4350; seeds 1-20 means 0.500, 0.496, 0.482, 0.434. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Seed 1: 0.5000, 0.4960, 0.4800, 0.4350; seeds 1-20 means 0.496, 0.482, 0.434.

claims.text: Watts and Strogatz's small-world model rewired ring links rather than adding new ones; this lesson adds shortcuts.
claims.source: D. J. Watts and S. H. Strogatz (1998), Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks, Nature 393: 440-442; the added-link variant is Newman and Watts (1999). NEEDS A HUMAN SOURCE CHECK (empirical/model source, not checked from the paper by the builder). Easley and Kleinberg 2010, ch. 20 section 20.2 (section number unconfirmed) discusses the model. The lesson attributes only the effect (few long links, short paths, high clustering) to Watts and Strogatz, not the added-link rule. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Watts and Strogatz (1998), Nature 393: 440-442: random rewiring of a ring lattice (Physics Today 1998 and networkx docs, via search). Newman and Watts (1999, arXiv cond-mat/9904419) abstract: "instead of rewiring each bond ... add shortcuts ... and do not remove lattice bonds". Reveal "(Watts and Strogatz rewired them)" is right. E&K ch. 20 is the small-world chapter (catalogue); section 20.2 stays unconfirmed.

claims.text: The ring's average of 12.9 steps (12.88) is the exact all-pairs value for 100 people who each know the 2 people on each side.
claims.source: Exact all-pairs BFS in model.ts averageSteps() over 100 x 99 ordered pairs gives 12.878787... = 1275/99. Check by hand: from one person the distance to the person k places away is ceil(k/2); k = 1..49 occurs twice (each side) and k = 50 once: 2 x 625 + 25 = 1275. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Own hand sum: 2 x sum_{k=1..49} ceil(k/2) + 25 = 2 x 625 + 25 = 1275; 1275/99 = 12.8788; matches averageSteps().

claims.text: A random network of this size and number of contacts would have clustering near 0.04.
claims.source: Approximation: in a random network the chance that two of a person's contacts know each other is about degree / N = 4 / 100 = 0.04. Each person in the ring has 4 contacts (2 each side), so degree = 4. Appears once, in the reveal's second paragraph ("a random network this size would sit near 0.04"); no mark on the stage. Approximation, not simulated by the builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Own simulation: 200 random G(100, 200 edges) graphs, mean local clustering 0.039; edge density 200/4950 = 0.040. "Near 0.04" holds. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-3): Stale source line re-read: the builder's source now says the 0.04 appears once, in reveal paragraph 2, with no stage mark. Confirmed in current Demo.tsx (RANDOM_LEVEL = 0.04, used only at line 129; no ghost mark or clustering readout on the stage). Status stays verified.

claims.text: 100 people who each know the 2 people on each side make 200 links.
claims.source: Each of 100 people has 2 links to the next people clockwise (ring distance 1 and 2): 100 x 2 = 200 links (ringEdges() length). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): ringEdges() gives 200 distinct pairs.

claims.text: Every pair a shortcut helps gets a shorter route, and nobody has to rewire the local circles.
claims.source: Adding a link never lengthens any shortest path (the old routes are still there), and a link between far-apart people gives every pair whose route can use it a shorter route. The lesson's model adds shortcuts to an unchanged ring (model.ts); it is a model, not a claim about real people. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Adding an edge cannot lengthen a shortest path; the model adds shortcuts to an unchanged ring. Read as "every pair a shortcut can help gets a shorter route", it holds. Advisory: "every route that can use it" could be read as any path through it; "every pair it helps" would be tighter. | REVISION v3: text changed to 'every pair a shortcut helps' as the fact-checker advised; back to unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. Adding an edge cannot lengthen any shortest path, and any pair whose distance falls did so via a shortcut; model.ts adds shortcuts to an unchanged ringEdges(). Wording 'every pair it helps' as advised in NCM-1.

claims.text: In the seed-1 world, the shortest route from person 3 to person 50 (labelled A and B) is 24 steps with no shortcuts, 5 with 5 shortcuts and 4 with 20 shortcuts (9 with 1).
claims.source: model.ts route(): BFS shortest path length from 3 to 50 on the ring plus the first 0, 1, 5, 20 shortcuts of the mulberry32(1) sequence. Re-run in node 2026-10-14 (builder): 24, 9, 5, 4. The pair was chosen as far apart on the ring and with falling length at every chip, not at random. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. Ran Demo.tsx route(c, 3, 50) on the current code: 24, 9, 5, 4 for 0, 1, 5, 20 shortcuts (ring distance 47 -> ceil(47/2) = 24). The reveal's hopsAt(0/5/20) = 24, 5, 4 are all reached states (milestones c5 and c20; 0 is the opening state).

recall.question: In a ring where everyone knows only their near neighbours, a few random long-distance links are added. What happens to the typical number of steps between two people?
recall.why: Each long link is a bridge between far-apart neighbourhoods, so many routes get much shorter, while most local friendships stay as they were.
